verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, with stringed instruments, a psalm, a song.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, to the strumming of strings: a psalm, and a song.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the heading, and in the Hebrew text it counts as verse 1, which is why the KJV's verse 1 is our verse 2. The heading is the stage direction. It names the leader of the music (the one the Targum calls the praiser, 'to praise'), the instruments, and two terms for the piece: a mizmor, a piece sung to plucked strings, and a shir, a general word for song. The two words together are rare (they occur together in a few headings, such as Psalms 48, 65, 66 and 68). The KJV renders the heading 'To the chief Musician on Neginoth', which keeps the Hebrew name nginot as if it were a tune, but the word means 'strings' or the playing of them. Ibn Ezra says he does not know who composed this psalm, and Radak and Meiri place it among the gathering of the exiles. Malbim ties it to the famine in David's time (2 Sam 21), which is a later tradition rather than anything in the heading. Do not play this as a solemn liturgy. The voices enter over strings.

philological_notes.note: A participle with a prefixed 'to': 'to the one who leads' or 'the choirmaster'. It heads 55 psalms. The root also means 'to be lasting' and 'to be pre-eminent', which is why the older versions thought of 'the victory' or 'the end'. Here it names the leader of the music.
'With stringed instruments': a plural of nginah, 'the playing of strings'. It is an accompaniment, not a tune name as the KJV's capitalized 'Neginoth' suggests.

verses.translation_literal: God, may he be gracious to us and may he bless us; may he make his face shine with us. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: God — let him be gracious to us, let him bless us. Let the light of his face rise and shine, here, among us. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: The opening is a prayer for the harvest as much as for the soul, and it echoes the priestly blessing of Numbers 6:24-26: 'bless', 'make his face shine', 'be gracious'. The singers take that blessing, said by priests over the people, and ask for it in their own mouths. The shining face is a common picture in the East: a king whose face shines is a king who is pleased, and whose subjects will eat. Rashi says it means to show a laughing face and to give dew and rain, so the shining is also the sun and the weather that make the crops come up. The KJV says 'upon us'; the Hebrew says 'with us', as if the light of that face stood beside the singers rather than beaming down on them from far away. The KJV also takes the verbs as wishes ('be merciful'), which is fair, but its 'merciful' is too heavy for the word chanan, which is the favor a patron grants to someone who has no claim on him. God appears as Elohim, not YHWH. This section of the Psalter prefers that title, so the singers pray to the God of all the world, which is the theme of what follows. Selah is a pause, perhaps for an instrument, perhaps for a raised voice. The meaning is unknown, so mark the beat and say nothing in it.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'or: 'cause to shine' or 'give light'. The idiom is of favor, a king looking kindly on his people, and in Numbers 6:25 it is the second blessing. Rashi reads it as a laughing face that gives dew and rain.
'May he show us favor': chanan is the undeserved kindness of one who has the power to withhold. Ibn Ezra links it to the similar uses of the same root elsewhere.
A musical or liturgical mark of unknown meaning, usually taken as a pause or lift. It is left untranslated.

token_glosses.gloss: may he be gracious to us

verses.translation_literal: To know on the earth your way, among all nations your salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: So that the earth may come to know your way; so that every nation may know the rescue you bring.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse gives the purpose of the blessing in verse 2: it is not only for us. The sentence has no verb of its own. It leans on the infinitive 'to know' and carries over from the prayer, so it reads as a purpose clause. Note the movement from a private prayer ('us') to the whole earth. The 'way' is the way God acts, his habit of conduct, as Rashi says (that his measure is to do good for his people), and 'salvation' is the concrete act of rescue, a harvest and a deliverance, not an afterlife. The KJV's 'saving health' is archaic and misleading: yeshuah is rescue and victory, and 'health' is only its old sense of well-being. It also adds 'upon earth' where the Hebrew has the plain 'in the earth' and sets it against 'among all nations'. Actors should hear the opening Hebrew word, la-da'at, as a goal reached across a distance.

philological_notes.note: 'Your way' means God's way of acting, his conduct, which others can watch. Rashi takes it as his habit of doing good to his people, Malbim as his justice and kindness together.
'Your salvation', meaning rescue or victory. The KJV's 'saving health' preserves an older meaning of 'health' as well-being and now reads as a medical term.

verses.translation_literal: May peoples praise you, God; may peoples praise you, all of them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the peoples praise you, God. Let the peoples praise you — every one of them.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the first of two identical lines, which form the refrain of the psalm: the same Hebrew appears again in verse 6, word for word. The repetition inside the verse ('may peoples praise you ... may peoples praise you') builds a rising crowd, and the final word, 'all of them', is what the singer reaches for. Perform it twice in the verse and again in verse 6 with a wider voice each time. The KJV says 'Let the people praise thee', with a singular 'people'. The Hebrew is plural, 'peoples', the other nations, not Israel alone. The KJV's 'people' hides what is radical here, that foreigners are asked to join Israel's thanksgiving. The verb is from yadah, 'to give thanks' and 'to confess', which is praise said aloud with the hands out, not only a feeling. Ibn Ezra and Radak read the line as the consequence of what came before: 'then' the peoples will praise.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of yadah, 'to throw' in the Qal and 'to give thanks, to praise, to confess' in the Hiphil. It is praise said aloud and in public, often with a gesture, and it is the root that gives 'Judah' its name in Genesis 29:35. The jussive reading ('may they') matches the other wishes in the psalm.
The plural 'peoples'. In the psalm it names the other nations, as 'goyim' does in verse 3. The KJV's 'the people' loses the plural.

verses.translation_literal: May they rejoice and may they sing for joy, nations, for you judge peoples on level ground, and nations on the earth you lead them. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the nations be glad. Let them cry out in joy, for you judge the peoples on level ground, and you lead the nations of the earth along the road. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: This verse supplies the reason for the world's praise, and the reason is a surprise: they sing because God judges. In a world of courts that could be bought, a judge who is fair is a reason for a cheer, and the nations are glad because for the first time they can expect a verdict that does not depend on their power. The word mishor means level, flat ground, a smooth road, and it is a metaphor for the equity of a judge, who does not tilt the case. The KJV's 'righteously' is a general term that flattens the picture, and its 'govern' for tanchem is too much a word of rule. The verb is nachah, 'to lead', the word used of a shepherd leading the flock (Psalm 23:3 has the same root), so the nations are led, not ruled. YLT's 'comfortest' confuses it with nacham, 'to comfort'. Follow the order of the Hebrew: the nations are glad, the peoples are judged on level ground, and the nations on the earth are led. The two verbs, 'judge' and 'lead', answer each other across the line, the bench and the road. Rashi says the leading is down a straight road, Metzudat David that it is a walking of the land in length and breadth in quiet and ease, and Radak and Malbim read it against the setting of the last war or a famine, but the text itself says only that God judges and leads. Selah closes the first half of the psalm.

philological_notes.note: 'Level ground', then 'evenness, equity': a judge who does not slope the case. It is the opposite of a crooked verdict. Metzudat Zion derives it from the root yashar, 'straight'.

Hiphil imperfect of nachah, 'to lead, to guide', with the suffix 'them'. It is the shepherd's verb, as in Psalm 23:3, and has nothing to do with nacham, 'to comfort', despite YLT's 'comfortest'. Rashi and Metzudat Zion gloss it as 'you lead them'.
'Nations', a poetic word that appears in both halves of the verse, beside 'ammim, 'peoples'. Meiri notes that it may also point to Israel, who are glad to see vengeance on the nations.

token_glosses.gloss: and may they sing for joy

verses.translation_literal: May peoples praise you, God; may peoples praise you, all of them.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let the peoples praise you, God. Let the peoples praise you — all of them, every one.
verses.directors_commentary: The refrain returns, word for word as in verse 4, and now it has a reason behind it: after the verdict in verse 5, the praise is earned. The same Hebrew, set after a new thought, should sound different, fuller and more sure. In verse 4 it was a wish thrown out toward the nations; here it is the answer to a God who has just been shown to be a fair judge. Ibn Ezra hears in it a second reason, that God makes the righteous right and the wicked wrong and settles the earth. Radak and Malbim tie it to future wars or to the rain that ended a drought. Keep the voice out of those private readings and let the line be the crowd. The KJV again has 'people' in the singular, though the Hebrew is the plural 'peoples'; it makes verses 4 and 6 identical to each other, which they are, but loses the point that the praise comes from many different nations.

philological_notes.note: 'All of them', a noun with a pronoun suffix and placed last for emphasis. It closes the line in the same way in verse 4.

verses.translation_literal: Earth has given its produce; may he bless us, God, our God.
verses.translation_dramatic: The earth has given. Its yield lies heaped and heavy in the hands of those who sowed. And now we ask for more than grain: let him bless us — God, our own God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns here from the nations to the field. 'Eretz' has been 'the earth' as the stage of the peoples' rule (verses 3 and 5); now it is soil, and it gives. In an agrarian economy of rain-fed grain, wine and oil, the yield (yevul) was the measure of whether God's favour was real. Radak reads the line against the background of drought sent for sin, and the earth's giving as a sign of restoration; Metzudat Zion glosses yevul simply as 'its fruit and growth'. Play the line as thanks and as proof, not as a bargain: the harvest comes first, and the blessing is asked on top of it.

The KJV's 'Then shall the earth yield her increase' turns a Hebrew perfect, 'has given', into a conditional future, and 'God, even our own God' inserts 'even' and 'own' that the Hebrew lacks. The Hebrew simply sets two words side by side, Elohim, Eloheinu: God, our God. The step from the universal word to the one with 'our' attached is the point. The God who judges the peoples with equity (verse 5) is the same one who belongs to this community, and the second word narrows the first, intimately and without fuss. The verb is the same barak that opens the psalm (verse 2), so the poem ends where it began, with the blessing asked in the first verse now wished again after the harvest.

philological_notes.note: 'Its produce', from yevul, the yield of field and tree, with the feminine suffix pointing back to 'eretz'. The root carries the sense of something brought in; the word is used for crops in Deut 11:17.

Two words for God in apposition: the general plural-form noun, then the same noun with the suffix 'our'. The pairing moves from God of all to God of us. Malbim reads 'our God' as God who watches over us in particular.

verses.translation_literal: May God bless us, and may all the ends of the earth fear him.
verses.translation_dramatic: God will bless us — and from every far edge of the earth, the whole world will stand in awe of him.
verses.directors_commentary: The last verse repeats the blessing a third time in a short compass (vv. 2, 7, 8) and then sends it as far as it will go: 'all the ends of the earth'. The picture is the edge of the known world, where the map stops. Those at the end of the world do not receive the blessing; they see it, and what they see makes them fear. The verb yare is fear in the sense of awe, holy respect, not terror, and the KJV's 'fear' is fine but needs the actor's care. Rashi voices the nations: 'Look at these who feared the Lord, how he blessed them and raised them!' Metzudat David says the far peoples fear because he watches and repays. The Hebrew does not say that the nations fear because they are afraid of being punished; it says only that God's blessing on his people is what draws them. The first verb, yevarekhenu, can be a wish ('may he bless') or a statement ('he will bless'), as in the KJV, ASV and BBE. The last verb, 'and may they fear', follows it and keeps the sense of purpose: blessing leads to awe. End the psalm on 'earth' with a long open vowel, and no Selah at the end, only silence.

philological_notes.note: 'The ends of the earth': afes is an end, a limit, the point at which something stops (and also 'nothing'). It marks the edge of the world as the ancients knew it. Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'ends'.
'And may they fear': awe before a power that is both great and kind. It is the response of the nations to what they see done for Israel, in Rashi's reading of the verse.
